sections.skill: Tell scheduled automation from model decisions and choose where each fits

questions.prompt: What is scheduled automation?

choices.text: Fixed rules that run at set times
A model that decides by itself what work to do each day, based on what seems important

questions.correct_answer: Fixed rules that run at set times
questions.intro: Not every automation needs a model to make choices. SCHEDULED AUTOMATION runs fixed rules at set times: "every Monday at 8, send the attendance report." It is PREDICTABLE: the same input gives the same result, and it is easy to test. MODEL-DECISION steps let a model choose something, such as which emails are urgent or what to reply. They handle messy situations rules cannot, but they can be wrong in surprising ways. A safe design uses fixed rules where the rule is clear, and model decisions only where judgment is needed, with checks around them.

sections.skill: Compare fixed automation and model decisions with a sprinkler timer and a gardener

questions.prompt: The sprinkler timer is like what?
questions.intro: A SPRINKLER TIMER waters the garden at 6 a.m. every day: predictable, cheap, and it never forgets, but it waters even when it is raining. A GARDENER looks at the plants and the weather and decides: flexible and smart, but sometimes wrong, and you want to know what they decided. Scheduled automation is the timer; a model decision is the gardener. Many gardens use both.

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Combine rules and model decisions safely

questions.prompt: A model chooses refunds and a fixed step pays automatically. What is the risk?

choices.text: No risk, because a fixed payment step always checks the model's decision before paying
A model error becomes a real payment

questions.correct_answer: A model error becomes a real payment
questions.intro: Mixing the two needs care. If a model decides which customers get a refund and a fixed step pays automatically, a model error becomes a real payment. Put model decisions where mistakes are cheap and reversible, or add a person before consequential steps. Also, fixed rules are not automatically safe: a wrong rule repeats its mistake every time. Test both kinds, and keep a record of what each step decided.

questions.prompt: How can that design be made safer?

choices.text: Add a person to approve before payment
Remove the fixed payment step and let the model send the payments directly by itself
